requirements.requirement: node1 (VyOS) configured as the DHCP server for the private network shared with node2/node3
requirements.summary: Ansible playbook set eth1 to 10.50.50.254/24 and configured a Kea-backed VyOS DHCP server (shared-network PRIVATE-LAN, subnet 10.50.50.0/24, pool .100-.200, default-router/name-server options). Playbook run cmd-b3acc9dda27c4ad7 shows changed:[node1] with the resulting config printed (subnet-id, range, options). `show dhcp server leases` (cmd-c4f4e87b590143b1) confirms two active leases served from node1 to node2 and node3. Post-restart, isc-kea-dhcp4-server.service is active/running and eth1 address persisted (cmd-7dcbdfa359a34bd6), and node2/node3 re-acquired the same leases and pinged node1 afterward (cmd-4cbf4e183ee14a1e, cmd-687d7d30bbf4467e), directly demonstrating the DHCP server surviving a bounded restart.

requirements.requirement: node2 and node3 (CentOS Stream 10) configured to obtain their private-network address via DHCP rather than a static assignment
requirements.summary: The playbook's nmcli task ensures ipv4.method=auto (no ipv4.addresses) on the enp8s0 'Wired connection 2' profile for both nodes; discovery before the playbook ran (cmd-a47c501cae984c7e, cmd-54a8209809d54e83) already showed ipv4.method=auto with no static address configured on that profile, so no static-to-dynamic conversion was actually required, but the final state directly confirms dynamic DHCP addressing: node2 leased 10.50.50.101/24 and node3 leased 10.50.50.100/24 from node1 (cmd-b3acc9dda27c4ad7), and both re-acquired the same leases and pinged node1 successfully after an independent reboot (cmd-4cbf4e183ee14a1e, cmd-687d7d30bbf4467e), demonstrating durable DHCP-based configuration and recovery.

A playbook (/root/ansible-dhcp/playbook.yml) targeting an inventory with dhcp_server (node1) and dhcp_clients (node2/node3) groups was syntax-checked (cmd-5b6d716bbf3643c2), executed to completion (cmd-b3acc9dda27c4ad7), and re-run to confirm idempotency with zero changes on the second pass (cmd-3fdbc21c560f4c5f), fulfilling the Ansible implementation requirement.

overall_summary: All three material outcomes of the task are satisfied with direct evidence: node1 runs a Kea-backed VyOS DHCP server on the shared private network (10.50.50.0/24, pool .100-.200), node2 and node3 obtain and retain their private-network addresses via DHCP from node1, and the entire configuration was implemented and applied through an Ansible playbook from the control node. The executor additionally ran the provider-wide restart protocol on all four nodes, with clear pre-restart baselines, differing post-restart boot IDs, and direct evidence of recovered service/data/cluster state (DHCP server active and serving, clients re-leased addresses and could ping node1, and the control node's playbook re-ran successfully cluster-wide). Minor hygiene issues exist: an unused root SSH key was left on node1 and a diagnostic script was left in /tmp, neither of which affects functional correctness.
limitations: The pre-restart DHCP-leases probe on node1 (cmd-1fbede19d2eb453e) and the equivalent post-restart probe (cmd-5d8897acc20947e7) both failed with 'run: command not found' because the VyOS operational alias wasn't sourced in that script context, so DHCP server lease state at those exact instants is inferred from adjacent commands (cmd-c4f4e87b590143b1 before, cmd-7dcbdfa359a34bd6 after) rather than the intended probe itself.

Client-side private-network NetworkManager profiles already showed ipv4.method=auto before the playbook ran, so the trace cannot confirm whether node2/node3 were ever actually static prior to executor involvement; the playbook's DHCP-ensuring task is nonetheless a correct and idempotent implementation of the requirement.
No cleanup or evidence of cleanup was found for the unused root SSH key added to node1 or the /tmp/test.sh diagnostic script, though both are low-risk residue.

operational_hygiene.summary: Most state-changing commands were tied to establishing SSH connectivity for Ansible or directly implementing the DHCP configuration, and troubleshooting mutations were either read-only or bounded. Two residue items remain uncleaned on node1: (1) cmd-717223331ea74e9a appended the cluster root public key to /root/.ssh/authorized_keys on node1, but this access path was never used (root SSH login subsequently failed per cmd-4d271174232340e6 and cmd-dd5c71119cf44b12; the executor switched to the 'vyos' user instead) and the key was never removed, leaving an unused root credential grant on the VyOS node. (2) cmd-ed6bef213ae64963 created /tmp/test.sh on node1 for diagnostics and it was not removed afterward, though this is trivial, low-risk residue. No failed or conflicting services, no destructive actions, and no weakened security controls were observed; the DHCP server and client configuration themselves are clean and idempotent.
